description: We are developing an intuitive tool to simplify lunar mission planning at the Moon’s south pole. It visualizes Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon, making it easy to assess solar power availability and direct-to-Earth communication windows for candidate landing sites. Join us to build next-gen tools for lunar exploration!
summary:
CELESTE is a browser-based navigator for lunar landing sites. Pick any site and date, and it shows where the Sun and Earth sit against that site's real terrain horizon. It also counts down to the next sunset or Earthset and shows which Deep Space Network antenna can reach the site. It covers 39 curated sites, including the 13 Artemis III candidate regions, plus custom coordinates. It can compare up to five sites side by side, and a date finder ranks the best landing dates. Skylines are traced on NASA LOLA elevation data down to 20 m resolution. The views include a 3D globe, south-polar terrain with GPU-computed shadows, horizon panoramas and timelines, and Earth-to-Moon flight reconstructions for 104 historical missions. Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.0045°. Three modes serve presenters, students and mission planners from the same validated numbers.

This matters because near the lunar south pole, moving a few kilometres can take a site from almost constant sunlight to permanent shadow. Sunlight decides how much power a lander gets, and line of sight to Earth decides whether it can communicate. CELESTE makes those trade-offs visible, measurable and easy to explain, using NASA's own data.
details:
What it does and how it works

CELESTE answers one question for any point on the Moon: from this spot, at this time, can you see the Sun, and can you talk to Earth? Choose a landing site and a date. CELESTE places the Sun and Earth against a 360° skyline traced from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data. Each skyline is 1,440 rays marched out to 350 km with the Moon's curvature handled exactly. The grid gets finer closer to the site, down to 20 m. From that skyline it computes:

  • sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset countdowns
  • solar elevation, the visible fraction of the Sun's disk and solar array output
  • line of sight to the Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra Deep Space Network stations

You can step, scrub or play time anywhere from 1960 to 2100. You can compare up to five sites, export event reports to CSV, or let the date finder score every possible landing date.

Benefits

  • Trustworthy: Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.0045°, checked against 1,620 samples from six sites. A suite of 43 automated tests checks known physical facts. For example, the floor of Shackleton crater never sees the Sun.
  • Honest: Every value shows where it came from, and areas with no terrain data are labelled "ideal sphere".
  • Easy to run: It needs no server, account or API key. It runs in any modern browser and can be hosted as a static site.

Intended impact

Near the lunar south pole, moving a few kilometres can take a site from nearly constant sunlight to total darkness. CELESTE makes that visible, so planners can reason about power and communications, and students and the public can understand why Artemis landing sites are chosen where they are. It has three modes:

  • Focus, for presenting
  • Explore, with plain-language explanations for learners
  • Mission control, with every readout for planners

All three modes use the same validated numbers.

Tools and technology

  • Languages and libraries: TypeScript, React, three.js and custom GLSL shaders, built with Vite and tested with Vitest. Astronomy Engine supplies the ephemeris, and Zustand holds the app state.
  • Data processing: Node.js scripts download and process NASA data. Playwright drives the screenshot and performance checks.
  • Data: NASA PDS LOLA elevation grids, the NASA GSFC PGDA south-pole site list, the LROC colour mosaic from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, NSSDCA landing coordinates, JPL Horizons and DSN antenna coordinates from DSN document 810-005.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. Performance was measured on an integrated Intel Iris Plus 655 GPU: about 60 fps on the globe and about 46 fps on the 80 m polar terrain with live shadows.
  • AI: AI coding assistants, mainly Anthropic's Claude, wrote much of the code under the team's direction. No AI-generated imagery or data is used.

Creativity

  • Shadows are ray-marched through the real height field on the GPU, so terrain lighting is computed, not painted.
  • A horizon scope shows the Sun and Earth disks at true scale against the skyline. Earth's monthly libration loop shows up in it.
  • Interactive flight reconstructions cover all 104 lunar missions ever launched, with 3D rocket models, staging and telemetry, and link to their landing sites.
  • The interface borrows proven ideas from professional tools: Blender's viewport and timeline, NASA GMAT's event reports and SODA's ground-station pass prediction.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy over appearance: Nothing on screen is decorative. Every readout and indicator is tied to a computed value.
  • Resolution: At the pole, position matters at the scale of the grid, so the finest available grid is used nearest each site.
  • Stated limits: The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no refraction term. DSN contact is geometric line of sight, not a link budget. Solar power counts direct sunlight only. Eclipses by Earth are not modelled.
  • Performance: Long calculations run in a Web Worker, positions are tabulated once and interpolated, and quality settings let lighter hardware run it.
  • Audience: Three modes let one tool serve experts and newcomers.
